transcript:
This message comes from Capital One with the Capital One Saver Card.
Earn unlimited 3% cash back on dining and entertainment.
Capital One. What's in your wallet? Terms apply. Details at CapitalOne.com.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman. President Trump's tariff policies will
be the focus today when a specialized trade court holds a hearing. As NPR Scott Horsley reports,
two previous efforts by the president to tax nearly all U.S. imports were found to be illegal.
Since July, President Trump has imposed double-digit tariffs on nearly all U.S.
imports in what the administration claims as a response to forced labor.
But opponents say the administration made no effort to differentiate between goods from
countries where forced labor is common and those where it's not. Critics say the forced labor claim
is a mere pretext, and the tariffs are really just a third attempt by the administration to
impose worldwide tariffs after two earlier rounds were struck down by the courts.
Several importers in nearly two dozen states are asking the Court of International Trade to
overturn these latest import taxes. They also want the court to order the Trump
administration to refund the money it's already collected. Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Officials at Cornell University are facing growing criticism over their handling of an alleged rape
case in 2024. NPR's Brian Mann reports New York Governor Kathy Hochul is calling for an
independent investigation. Hochul called a woman's account of being drugged and gang-raped at Cornell
in 2024 horrifying. She says there are serious questions and is calling for a transparent,
independent review of the university's response. A local prosecutor says the alleged victim described
parts of the incident as consensual at the time, but potential evidence of violence by seven male
students was only investigated by campus police, not by city police. Ithaca's mayor Robert Cantelmo
has also blasted Cornell's response. In a statement to NPR, Cornell University says it will work with
elected officials to address safety concerns. They didn't say whether they will approve an
independent investigation. Ryan Mann, NPR News, Ithaca, New York. The artificial intelligence
company, OpenAI, has launched an AI-enabled bot that its chat GPT users can now start using.
This bot is called DOTS, and it arrives as concerns about safety with AI spiral. NPR's
John Ruich reports OpenAI has said other of its AI bots hacked websites and did other things they
weren't supposed to do during training runs. OpenAI's new agent will be able to do a range of tasks
for users from managing email to fixing computer code. The release fell on the same day that
industry leaders met with President Trump in Washington after a chorus of calls for an AI
development slowdown to make sure humans don't lose control of the technology. OpenAI President Greg
Brockman went to Washington, so CEO Sam Altman could be in San Francisco for the launch of DOTS
at the company's developer conference. Altman says he hopes the AI industry can forge a sensible middle
path between those pushing development at all costs and those calling for an end to the technology.
John Ruich, NPR News. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The Pentagon says Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is going to announce more cuts to the number
of generals and admirals serving in the U.S. military. He has already ordered a 10 percent
cut to the flag and general officer positions. Hegseth will now double that to a 20 percent cut
by the end of the year. The mammoth farm bill is set to expire at the end of the day today.
Congress is deadlocked over the next version of the legislation typically passed every five years.
The program supports agriculture and the current U.S. economy is already dire for many of the
nation's farmers. A FEMA-backed program is running out of money. It has helped hundreds of survivors
of last year's Los Angeles fires navigate the rebuilding process. NPR's Kirk Siegler has more.
As is typical after bad wildfires, last year FEMA approved 13 million dollars toward its disaster
case management program, which pairs a case manager to fire survivors like Sophia Vidal,
helping them with insurance, securing building permits, and a grant so that her husband, who's a
contractor, could replace his tools that burned in the fire. We need her guidance to help us get
back on track as far as what we need to do next. But Vidal and some 1,300 other survivors are now
losing their case managers, as only 3 million of the promise 13 million in aid has actually been
distributed in the L.A. burn zones. FEMA also recently denied an aid request for an additional
6 million, which California leaders say is further delaying a slow recovery. Kirk Siegler reporting.
This is NPR. Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks? Amazon Prime members can listen

Cornell University faces criticism from Governor Hochul over handling of alleged 2024 rape case
OpenAI launches DOTS, an AI-enabled bot for ChatGPT users amid safety concerns
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to announce doubling of military general and admiral cuts to 20 percent
Farm bill set to expire end of day as Congress remains deadlocked on next version
FEMA disaster case management program running out of money for Los Angeles fire survivors
